title: Whose is it? — possession and family
goal: Show possession with the ending -র · -এর, introduce your family — and discover that Bengali has no verb “to have” at all.
bekal: attach the possessive ending -র · -এর to names and nouns
know আমার, তোমার, আপনার, তার, আমাদের by heart
tell আমার আছে apart from আমার কাছে আছে
name family members with the right word

dialogs.title: কথোপকথন — Opening the photo album
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon: Mitali opens the family photo album in the living room. Watch for the endings -র and -এর, which turn up in almost every line: they are what this whole unit is about.

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: It's a photo of our family. An old photo.
lines.literal: this — our — family's — photo. old — photo.

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: No, this is my grandmother. My mother's mother.
lines.literal: no, this — my — grandmother(mother's side). mother's — mother.

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: Ha ha, that's Rahim! He was seven back then.
lines.literal: ha ha, that — rahim — brother! his — age — then — seven.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Do you have any other brothers or sisters?

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: We have an older sister. Her name is Shirin.
lines.literal: our — one — big — sister — exists. her — name — shirin.

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: Shirin's home is in Sylhet. Her husband works there.
lines.literal: shirin — sister's — home — sylhet-in. there — her — husband — work — does.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Do you have any new photos of them?
lines.literal: your(polite) — near — [Q] — their — new — photo — exists?

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: On my phone! Just a moment, I'll show you.

notes: **Possession takes one ending: -এর after a consonant, -র after a vowel.** রহিম → **রহিমের** বই (Rahim's book). মিতালি → **মিতালির** ঘর (Mitali's room). বাবা → **বাবার** চশমা (Father's glasses). The order is exactly like English *'s*: owner first, then the thing owned.

⚠️ **Two endings can stack, always in the same order: possessive first, place second.** রহিম + এর + বাড়ি + তে = **রহিমের বাড়িতে** (“Rahim's house-at” = at Rahim's house). Once you get used to stacking, long Bengali sentences stop looking scary — they are just a chain of words, each carrying its own ending.

**The possessive pronouns must be memorized, because they are not fully regular.** আমি → **আমার**, আমরা → **আমাদের**, তুমি → **তোমার**, আপনি → **আপনার**, সে → **তার**, তিনি → **তাঁর**, ও → **ওর**, তারা → **তাদের**. ⚠️ Note **তার** (his/her, plain) versus **তাঁর** (his/her, polite, with chandrabindu) — one small nasal mark separates polite from impolite.

⚠️ **Bengali has no verb “to have”.** For “I have a book”, people say **আমার একটা বই আছে** — literally “my a book exists”. The subject of the sentence is the **book**, not the person. That is why the negative uses নেই too: আমার বই **নেই** (I don't have a book). English uses a verb “have”; Bengali says “with me there is”.

**There are two ways to say “have”, and the difference is real.** **আমার … আছে** is for things that **belong** to you — family, a house, a trait, an illness: আমার একটা বোন আছে. **আমার কাছে … আছে** (literally “near me there is”) is for something you **have on you**: আমার কাছে টাকা আছে (I have money on me). ⚠️ Saying *আমার টাকা আছে* means “I'm well-off”, not “I've got cash on me” — a difference that can make a market chat quite funny.

**Bengali kinship words are far more detailed than English ones.** An uncle on your **father's** side is চাচা *chacha*, on your **mother's** side মামা *mama*. An aunt on the father's side is ফুফু *phuphu*, on the mother's side খালা *khala*. Grandparents differ too: দাদা · দাদি on the father's side, নানা · নানি on the mother's side. ⚠️ Just saying “uncle” is not enough; people will ask back “which uncle?”

⚠️ **দাদা has two meanings, and this is a real trap.** In Bangladesh **দাদা** means **paternal grandfather**. In West Bengal (Kolkata) দাদা means **older brother**, and it is used every day to address a man slightly older than you — like calling someone “brother”. Place and context decide; if in doubt, use **ভাই**, which is safe everywhere.

grammars.title: Pronouns and their possessive forms
after: **For ordinary nouns, the rule fits on one line:** ends in a consonant → **-এর** (দেশ → দেশের, বাজার → বাজারের); ends in a vowel → **-র** (মিতালি → মিতালির, বাবা → বাবার, ছেলে → ছেলের).
**কার?** *kar* means “whose?” — the possessive of কে (who). এটা কার বই? = “Whose book is this?”

grammars.title: Family — পরিবার
after: ⚠️ **স্ত্রী *stri* is a wife, but ইস্ত্রি *istri* is a clothes iron.** One little vowel i in front turns your spouse into a household appliance. If in doubt, use the safer everyday word: **বউ** *bou* (wife).

blocks.text: These five sentences are enough to answer questions about your family — and you will be asked, because it is the second thing Bengalis ask after your name.

head: Sentence
Say it
Meaning
rows: There are five of us in my family.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Questions that may surprise you
items: **আপনি কি বিবাহিত?** (*ap-ni ki bi-ba-hi-tô*) — “Are you married?” In Bengal this is ordinary small talk, not a personal question, and it's fine to ask someone you've just met. A safe answer: **হ্যাঁ** or **না, এখনো না** (not yet).
**আপনার বয়স কত?** (*ap-nar bô-yôsh kôt*) — “How old are you?” Also considered normal. If you'd rather not answer, smile and say **আন্দাজ করুন** (take a guess) — it works well.

**আপনার দেশ কোথায়?** — “Where is your country?” Answer **আমি ইন্দোনেশিয়া থেকে** (or name your own country), then get ready: many Bengalis will have something to say about it right away — cricket, football, a cousin who lives there.

blocks.text: One custom worth understanding. In Bengal, family is not just parents and children. **আত্মীয়** *atmiyô* — relatives — covers a much wider circle, and cousins are often called ভাই and বোন with no qualifier at all. If someone introduces ten people as their “brothers and sisters”, they are not exaggerating; that is simply how the words are used.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the correct possessive pronoun.
Put the words in the right order.

items: Do you have money on you?

answers: আমার একটা বোন আছে। — আমার কোনো ভাই নেই। — আমার কাছে টাকা আছে। — এই বইটা কার? — শিরিন আপার পরিবার সিলেটে থাকেন।
এটা কার বই? — আমার দুই ভাই আছে। — আমার কোনো বোন নেই। — রহিমের বাড়ি ঢাকায়। — আমার মায়ের নাম সিতি। — আপনার কাছে কি টাকা আছে?
